I just wanted to update this ticket because I wanted to start 'fresh' to see what the actual issue is. In my [original comment](https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/issues/5#issue-976311622), I mentioned that I needed to do the following:

1. Authorize the OAuth consumer to my account by visiting https://bitbucket.org/site/oauth2/authorize?client_id=<client_id>&response_type=code once - fill in your client_id from the OAuth consumer creation step.

I was incorrect, and this is an unnecessary step. I looked more closely at what the underlying [githosts-utils library](https://github.com/jonhadfield/githosts-utils/blob/master/bitbucket.go#L19) was doing, and it's using the client_credentials grant. To enable this, you do need to select the *This is a private consumer* option when creating the OAuth consumer. 

With that said, I still do need to set the user to x-token-auth instead of my actual username. 

One thing to note is that even with the client_credentials grant, I only was able to access the public/private repositories in the workspace where I created the OAuth consumer. I couldn't find anything in the BitBucket docs that indicated if that was by design - even when I opened up the scopes of the OAuth consumer. I can get around this by just creating consumers in each workspace, but one idea may be to support app passwords instead of the key/secret dance which would simplify a bit of this.

Thanks for all your work on this!
No problem. Thanks for reporting the issue.
IIRC, the reason I implemented this flow was due to the issue of 2FA preventing unattended runs. The app password appears to get around that constraint, so I'll look to add this as an option.

I think it'll require extra configuration; You can be a member of many organisations, so it could result in a user cloning hundreds or thousands of repositories. I want to keep this as simple as possible, with a few env vars for config, but will take a look to see what's possible.

The alternative is to retrieve Projects by minimum access level, so I've switched the behaviour in my code and proven this works as I can now clone repositories from another user where I have a Project access level of at least Reporter (I spent a lot of time wondering why Guest wasn't sufficient, until I RTFM).  
The previous env var is now replaced with: GITLAB_PROJECT_MIN_ACCESS_LEVEL as the filter, where the value is an integer as follows:  
```
20: "Reporter"
30: "Developer"
40: "Maintainer"
50: "Owner"
```
If unset, the default is 20.

Just a heads-up.  
I've pushed a new beta that replaces the SOBA_DEV trigger with:  
- GITHUB_COMPARE
- GITLAB_COMPARE
- BITBUCKET_COMPARE   

each supporting a value of either 'refs' or 'clone' where 'clone' is the default if not specified.  
refs = check latest bundle refs (if existing bundle exists) against remote refs, without cloning  
clone = clone the remote, bundle it, and compare latest bundle size and checksum with local (if existing bundle exists)  

The reason for defaulting to clone is that someone's pointed out that using refs alone doesn't consider the remote could be shallow (older commits removed). I doubt it's a common situation, but don't want to make any assumptions when it comes to backups.

Hi, What use-case are you thinking of?  
Not sure I can see the benefit whilst it's not listening on a port, like a webserver.

I'm not sure if it can be done, but I'd love to know if the service/"cronjob" is still running. Not sure if it always exists with an error code if there is an issue?
If it's not really necessary, feel free to close ^^

Makes sense. I run the docker image on a Synology NAS that you can configure to Auto Restart if the process ends.
One approach to running with cron is to use flock: https://serverfault.com/a/82863/463326.  You could set the cron to run every minute (as in the serverfault example) so it automatically restarts if it fails and can check the existence of the lock file to know if it's running.

soba will exit with `1` if there's an error and `0` if you run it once (without a backup interval) and it succeeds.

Oh, sorry, I think I phrased that the wrong way.
I'm also using the docker image on a Synology NAS (together with Portainer, but that's not important I presume) and I just set the GIT_BACKUP_INTERVAL to a certain hours value (that's what I meant with "cronjob").
However, I think you're right, just being on the lookout for that `1` error code is probably enough. Seems like I didn't think this through.
Thanks a lot for your extensive answer anyway! I love this image, keep up the awesome work <3

Hi @xXluki98Xx,  
Yes, the instructions linked to are for using the API to get tokens, but I should have provided more user-friendly instructions, as I have for the other providers.  
I'll update/add a link shortly.  
In the meantime, after logging into the Gitea web interface, click on your user icon in the top right-hand corner and go to `Settings`. From there, choose `Application`. Add a token name, e.g. "RepoBackups".  
Expand the `Select permissions` list and then select Organisation Read and Repo Read permissions. _Let me know if you get any errors with that_.  
Then click on `Generate Token` and you'll see some text at the top of the screen like this: `7d1aa88124c304dbbd5cbbf41766e0a2fe03ff0a`.  That's the value you need to set for environment variable `GITEA_TOKEN`. For `GITEA_APIURL` use: `https://my.domain.com/api/v1`.  

Hope this helps, and thanks for the feedback.

performed_via_github_app.name: SonarQubeCloud
performed_via_github_app.description:
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) is a SaaS code analysis tool designed to detect coding issues in 30+ languages, frameworks, and IaC platforms. Your code is checked against an extensive set of rules that cover many attributes of code, such as maintainability, reliability, and security issues, on each merge/pull request.

For those requiring US-based hosting, [SonarQube Cloud US](https://sonarqube.us/) offers the perfect alternative. If you need data residency outside the US or within the EU, [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/) with this GitHub app is the ideal solution.

SonarQube Cloud integrates seamlessly into your GitHub workflow and provides clear guidance for resolving any code quality and security issues detected. The majority of popular languages can be analyzed automatically; no configuration is required!

With [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/github), you get:

-   Fast, precise static analysis and feedback on your code
    
-   Support for popular languages, frameworks, and IaC tools
    
-   Free analysis for open-source projects and private projects up to max 50k LoC
    
-   Automatic analysis of pull requests and branches with results reported inline
    
-   IDE Support with [SonarQube for IDE](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarlint/) integration
    
-   Quality Gate (added as a GitHub check) acting at two different levels - first, preventing you from merging pull requests that contain issues - and later, helping you to release only clean, safe code
    
-   Sign up for SonarQube free tier and begin scanning your private and public repositories
    

A [GitHub Action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/sonarcloud-scan) is available in the marketplace to make it easy for you (for projects where automatic analysis isn't available). SonarQube Cloud also integrates smoothly with Jenkins, CircleCI, TravisCI, CirrusCI, and many other tools.

A free tier is available that allows you to explore the benefits of SonarQube Cloud using your public and private repositories. We also provide a no-commitment, [14-day trial](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarcloud/signup/) of SonarQube Cloud Team for unlimited team members, up to 1.9M LoC, AI CodeFix recommendations, and more. No need to speak with a sales rep or request a license key - get automatic code analysis results on your private projects in minutes! Want to see more examples of SonarCloud in action? You can [explore current Open Source projects in SonarCloud](https://sonarcloud.io/explore/projects?sort=-analysis_date) that are using the [Clean as You Code](https://www.sonarsource.com/solutions/our-unique-approach/) methodology.

What are you waiting for? SonarQube Cloud helps you consistently deliver cleaner, secure software that future developers will appreciate and your users will love. Start writing Clean Code. [Now](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarcloud/signup/)!

Hi, thanks for the feedback.
I'll take a look asap.

Hi, I've done some testing and found that it's not just a missing callback URL that causes an issue, but also if the following option isn't checked:
```
[ ] This is a private consumer
Enables the client_credentials grant type. Installable applications that ship their OAuth consumer credentials as part of the application should not be marked as private. 
```
The difference with BitBucket and the other providers is that BitBucket returns an HTTP 200 (Success) response when there's an auth failure response, so soba continued as if nothing was wrong. 

I've modified a dependency https://github.com/jonhadfield/githosts-utils/commit/f5981bc0a6ec4a2a69fb25a892ceb4565c640269 to ensure any errors are captured and returned.
...and put out a new release: https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/releases/tag/1.2.7

Without callback uri defined:  
`soba: 2024/01/16 11:22:55 bitbucket.go:226: failed to get bitbucket auth token: invalid_request - No callback uri defined for the OAuth client.`

Without setting OAuth consumer as a private consumer:  
`soba: 2024/01/16 11:22:27 bitbucket.go:226: failed to get bitbucket auth token: invalid_grant - Cannot use client_credentials with a consumer marked as "public". Calls for auto generated consumers should use urn:bitbucket:oauth2:jwt instead.`

I'll put a note in the documentation also.

Thanks again for flagging, and let me know if you notice any issues.
thanks, works great!
I've just updated documentation to include Kubernetes cron job setup instructions, and added sample manfifest files.

Hi @r3mi, I think to know the runtime status should rely on checking the logs. Simply because the alternative would require exposing an endpoint and therefore an attack vector that could be exploited. It also adds more complexity, more work for the user (ssl certs etc.), and a lot more work to maintain (patch) and test the codebase.  
A notification of success/failure makes sense though: email, sms, push notification or, as you suggest, a webhook. I'll take a look at implementing a webhook and see if I can put it out in a release asap.  

Thanks for your feedback and suggestion.

thanks. 
Some thoughts, if it makes sense:
- would be best to be able to configure separate hooks for success vs failure : typically I would send success to a heartbeat monitor, and failure to an alert system
- would be nice to have some flexibility on the webhook format/destination, for example through using https://github.com/containrrr/shoutrrr or equivalent

Thanks for having a look !

Thanks, this is useful and looks very well done !
Sending a webhook is the most interesting part you are right. My suggestions (eg separate success / failure) are just nice-to-have and not major.
I can not test the beta in my setting easily (I use the docker image), but your description looks fine.
Thanks for the quick answers and work !
I've got a few bits to tidy up and test, but will try and get a new release out asap.
New release, including docker image, now out: https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/releases/tag/1.2.8
Documentation now updated so closing issue.

Hi, from a basic cli sense, I wanted to just print the error and exit. That way the user has their feedback and can correct before trying again.  That logic allowed me to output errors (and store for webhook summaries) and continue running for non-catastrophic issues.
I see how this isn't a good fit for running something wrapped in some logic that says "on error, do it again asap". For obvious reasons, I don't include any code to report back to me (even anonymously) how this app is used or when and why it errors, so it's impossible to know the priority, nor impact, of attempting to improve this logic.  I may look to make that an explicit opt-in feature (no nagging in the app etc., but something mentioned in the README.md) in future.
I've had a look at the code base and it's a non-trivial change that could take some time to implement behaviour that caters for CLI, Cron, Kubernetes Cron, and Docker-Compose users. It's daunting to think of how to even automate testing for all those scenarios, but I know it's a must.  
Whilst it makes sense to send a Webhook if the app does fail, I'm also conscious of thrashing your web hook receiver, so first need to work out how to ensure a delay after quick exit.   

Please excuse the rambling. I think the tl;dr version is: I'll work on it, but it'll take time, and would it be possible to use a [restart policy](https://github.com/compose-spec/compose-spec/blob/master/deploy.md#restart_policy) on docker-compose in the meantime?

Yes, I did that : `restart: on-failure:3`  to avoid being stuck in a failed auth loop, and then I can be alerted from monitoring tools.
Thanks for the explanation!

Makes sense. What's odd is the query I'm running should only return: "A list of repositories that the user owns". I've tested and it does still return those I collaborate on.  
I don't want to make a breaking change, i.e. limiting to user owned by default, so thinking the simplest implementation would be a boolean: yes/no(default) on new env var: `GITHUB_USER_OWNED` where I run an additional filter to limit to repos where your login/username is the repository owner.  
It doesn't prevent me adding `GITHUB_OWNERS` later on, but that will take a bit more work to get right.

Thanks for the consideration. And thanks for the project. Im glad for your active maintenance.

I think the repos returned has to do with GitHub's classic access token having too broad permissions. Implementing the new access tokens would probably help but I know those are more complicated. 

Thanks again.

Thanks for your feedback. Really appreciate it.  

I directly use the newer GraphQL (rather than REST) API and a limitation was that it only supported classic tokens. It's now caught up and supports the fine grained personal access tokens too. I did have a play with it, with a PAT only allowing access to specific repos, but what happens is it still returns all the non-private repos you're affiliated with, so not quite what you're after.   
I've worked out how to get the user owned only (minor query change) so will use that version of the query if you set `GITHUB_USER_OWNED` to `yes`. Will get a release out asap.

> with a PAT only allowing access to specific repos, but what happens is it still returns all the non-private repos you're affiliated with

Hoo boy. I see why they're coming up with a new system.

> Will get a release out asap.

Thanks!

New release pushed: https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/releases/tag/1.2.12  
I opted for `GITHUB_LIMIT_USER_OWNED` in the end. Set that to true and it should do what you need.
Already got it in installed and it's working great. Thanks again!

Hi @r3mi,
I've put out [1.2.14](https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/releases/tag/1.2.14) that hopefully addresses the error handling and api thrashing.  
In case of any initial failures like provider authentication, I collect the error and let the other providers continue. On completion, the webhook will now contain the error, plus the error stack to show where in the code it failed.  
If soba's running non-daemonized, it should now also return the correct exit code, i.e. 0 for success and 1 for failure.
thanks ! works fine !

Hi @r3mi, sorry for the delay.
A common way to pull env vars is from a file, i.e. create a file called .env containing your definitions:

    GITHUB_TOKEN=xyz
    GITLAB_TOKEN=abc

And then the app reads that on startup. I can quite simply add that feature and was something I intended to do anyhow.

When using docker secrets in a compose file, it seems I'd need to add support for each of the env vars with secrets: GITHUB_TOKEN, GITLAB_TOKEN, etc. to have the equivalent GITHUB_TOKEN_FILE, GITLAB_TOKEN_FILE, etc. That shouldn't be too much effort to support. In the case of GITHUB_TOKEN vs GITHUB_TOKEN_FILE both being set, I'll flag it as an error rather than make an assumption on which one to use.

Thank you. Yes that is the second option I was referring to (`xxx_FILE` env var, compatible with docker compose secrets). That would be great.
For the `.env` file, I can already load it automatically as needed, through docker compose mechanisms.

body: Great news! thx

Really sorry. I've misunderstood instructions from BitBucket in that "App Passwords" are being discontinued, so I switched auth to using API Keys. I now realise that oauth2 isn't going anywhere.  I'll try and reinstate oauth2 and leave API Keys as an option.    

If you want to use the new version, then API keys are managed here: https://id.atlassian.com/manage-profile/security/api-tokens (better you search on your account than trust that URL from a random person on the internet though).  You just need scopes: `read:project:bitbucket` and `read:repository:bitbucket` then set env var: `BITBUCKET_EMAIL` with your email address and `BITBUCKET_API_TOKEN` with the token.

I'll update docs now and work on a fix asap.

no worry, I don't mind switching ! but I didn't catch the change in the README.
The API token seems more friendly to setup.

Tested 1.3.7 with API token, but I have 2 issues:

1) fails with _FILE variables

```
soba: 2025/06/29 14:21:14 bitbucket.go:94: listing BitBucket repositories
soba: 2025/06/29 14:21:14 bitbucket.go:127: unexpected status code: 401 Unauthorized (401)
```
I defined
```
      BITBUCKET_EMAIL_FILE: /run/secrets/BITBUCKET_EMAIL
      BITBUCKET_API_TOKEN_FILE: /run/secrets/BITBUCKET_API_TOKEN
 ```

I suspect <https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/blob/5f3ee55739a963640250fe199f06b8f0ed25b073/internal/bitbucket.go#L46> should be something like bbToken and bbemail , not os.getenv ?

2) do not backup all repos

(I used the regular non-FILE variables to get successful auth)

it works but only backup the first 10 repos from my default workspace.

Thanks so much for the feedback.  
Life is getting in the way of me getting this fixed quickly. Hope to have it sorted on the weekend.

I believe this is now fixed in [release 1.3.8](https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/releases/tag/1.3.8).  
OAuth now works again, and if you specify both API token auth "and" OAuth, it will default to API token.

### Code Review for Claude Code GitHub Workflow PR

I've reviewed the merged PR that adds Claude Code integration workflows. Here's my comprehensive analysis:

- [x] Read and analyze `.github/workflows/claude-code-review.yml`
- [x] Read and analyze `.github/workflows/claude.yml` 
- [x] Evaluate security considerations
- [x] Check GitHub Actions best practices
- [x] Assess potential bugs or issues
- [x] Provide constructive feedback

## Review Summary

### ✅ **Strengths**

**Security Best Practices**
- Proper use of GitHub secrets for API tokens (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`)
- Minimal required permissions with principle of least privilege
- Use of `id-token: write` for secure token handling
- No hardcoded sensitive values

**Code Quality & Structure**
- Clean, well-organized YAML structure
- Comprehensive inline comments explaining configuration options
- Good use of conditional triggers to prevent unnecessary runs
- Proper checkout action with minimal fetch depth for performance

**Flexibility & Configuration**
- Extensive commented examples for customization
- Support for different models (Sonnet 4, Opus 4)
- Configurable prompts and tool permissions
- Multiple trigger patterns (mentions, assignments, etc.)

### 🔧 **Areas for Improvement**

**Minor Issues**
1. **claude-code-review.yml:32** - `fetch-depth: 1` might be insufficient for review context
   - Consider `fetch-depth: 0` or `fetch-depth: 10` for better diff analysis
   
2. **claude.yml:31** - Same fetch depth concern for comprehensive code analysis

**Best Practice Suggestions**
1. **Error Handling** - No explicit error handling or fallback mechanisms
2. **Rate Limiting** - No protection against excessive Claude invocations
3. **Workflow Naming** - Could benefit from more descriptive job names

**Performance Considerations**
1. Both workflows use `ubuntu-latest` which is appropriate
2. Minimal permissions are correctly configured
3. Single fetch depth is good for performance but might limit review quality

### 🛡️ **Security Assessment**

**Excellent Security Posture:**
- No security vulnerabilities identified
- Proper secret management
- Appropriate permission scoping
- No exposure of sensitive data

**Permissions Analysis:**
```yaml
# claude-code-review.yml permissions: ✅ Minimal
contents: read        # Repository access
pull-requests: read   # PR metadata
issues: read         # Issue access  
id-token: write      # OIDC token

# claude.yml permissions: ✅ Minimal + CI integration
+ actions: read      # CI results access
```

### 📋 **Test Coverage**

**Missing Test Considerations:**
- No validation of workflow syntax (could add workflow linting)
- No integration tests for Claude responses
- Consider adding workflow dispatch triggers for testing

### 🚀 **Recommendations**

1. **Enhance Fetch Depth** - Consider deeper history for better context:
   ```yaml
   fetch-depth: 10  # or 0 for full history
   ```

2. **Add Rate Limiting** - Consider workflow concurrency controls:
   ```yaml
   concurrency:
     group: claude-${{ github.event.number || github.sha }}
     cancel-in-progress: true
   ```

3. **Error Handling** - Add step-level error handling for better debugging

## 🎯 **Overall Assessment**

This is a **high-quality implementation** that follows GitHub Actions best practices. The workflows are well-structured, secure, and provide excellent flexibility through comprehensive configuration options. The extensive inline documentation makes it easy for maintainers to customize behavior.

The implementation successfully enables Claude Code integration while maintaining security and following best practices. The commented configuration options provide excellent guidance for future customization.

### Investigating Intermittent GitHub Failures ✅

I've completed my analysis of the intermittent GitHub backup failures where you're seeing `backup failed: <nil>` errors.

**Todo List:**
- [x] Check for repository-specific guidelines (CLAUDE.md)
- [x] Examine the codebase structure
- [x] Analyze github.go around line 543 where the error occurs
- [x] Understand the backup failure logic and error handling
- [x] Identify root cause of nil errors
- [x] Propose improvements for better error handling

### Root Cause Analysis

**The Problem:**
The error `backup failed: <nil>` originates from the `github.com/jonhadfield/githosts-utils` library (version `v0.0.0-20250705185938-cbe1c782cb3e`), not from soba directly. This happens when:

1. **Error Source**: The error is logged within the githosts-utils library at line 543 of its github.go file
2. **Nil Error Issue**: The `<nil>` indicates that an error occurred but no specific error details were captured or properly propagated
3. **Intermittent Nature**: This typically occurs due to:
   - Network timeouts or connectivity issues
   - GitHub API rate limiting (HTTP 403/429 responses)
   - Authentication token issues
   - Race conditions in concurrent operations

### Proposed Improvements

While the core issue is in the githosts-utils dependency, here are several ways soba can improve error handling and debugging:

**1. Enhanced Logging Context**
- Add more contextual information before calling `githubHost.Backup()` in `/home/runner/work/soba/soba/internal/github.go:53`
- Log GitHub API configuration details (org count, compare method, etc.) to help correlate failures

**2. Error Recovery Strategy**
- Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for GitHub backup failures
- Add circuit breaker pattern to prevent cascading failures

**3. Better Error Propagation**
- Capture and wrap errors with more context about the backup operation that failed
- Add structured logging with error categories

**4. Monitoring Improvements**
- Add metrics for different types of failures (nil errors, timeout errors, API errors)
- Include more details in webhook notifications when errors occur

### Immediate Actions You Can Take

1. **Update githosts-utils**: Check if a newer version fixes the nil error issue

For those requiring US-based hosting, [SonarQube Cloud US](https://sonarqube.us/) offers the perfect alternative. If you need data residency outside the US or within the EU, [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/) with this GitHub app is the ideal solution.

SonarQube Cloud integrates seamlessly into your GitHub workflow and provides clear guidance for resolving any code quality and security issues detected. The majority of popular languages can be analyzed automatically; no configuration is required!

With [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/github), you get:

-   Fast, precise static analysis and feedback on your code
    
-   Support for popular languages, frameworks, and IaC tools
    
-   Free analysis for open-source projects and private projects up to max 50k LoC
    
-   Automatic analysis of pull requests and branches with results reported inline
    
-   IDE Support with [SonarQube for IDE](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarlint/) integration
    
-   Quality Gate (added as a GitHub check) acting at two different levels - first, preventing you from merging pull requests that contain issues - and later, helping you to release only clean, safe code
    
-   Sign up for SonarQube free tier and begin scanning your private and public repositories
    

A [GitHub Action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/sonarcloud-scan) is available in the marketplace to make it easy for you (for projects where automatic analysis isn't available). SonarQube Cloud also integrates smoothly with Jenkins, CircleCI, TravisCI, CirrusCI, and many other tools.

A free tier is available that allows you to explore the benefits of SonarQube Cloud using your public and private repositories. performed_via_github_app.name: SonarQubeCloud
performed_via_github_app.description:
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) is a SaaS code analysis tool designed to detect coding issues in 30+ languages, frameworks, and IaC platforms. Your code is checked against an extensive set of rules that cover many attributes of code, such as maintainability, reliability, and security issues, on each merge/pull request.

For those requiring US-based hosting, [SonarQube Cloud US](https://sonarqube.us/) offers the perfect alternative. If you need data residency outside the US or within the EU, [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/) with this GitHub app is the ideal solution.

SonarQube Cloud integrates seamlessly into your GitHub workflow and provides clear guidance for resolving any code quality and security issues detected. The majority of popular languages can be analyzed automatically; no configuration is required!

With [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/github), you get:

-   Fast, precise static analysis and feedback on your code
    
-   Support for popular languages, frameworks, and IaC tools
    
-   Free analysis for open-source projects and private projects up to max 50k LoC
    
-   Automatic analysis of pull requests and branches with results reported inline
    
-   IDE Support with [SonarQube for IDE](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarlint/) integration
    
-   Quality Gate (added as a GitHub check) acting at two different levels - first, preventing you from merging pull requests that contain issues - and later, helping you to release only clean, safe code
    
-   Sign up for SonarQube free tier and begin scanning your private and public repositories
    

A [GitHub Action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/sonarcloud-scan) is available in the marketplace to make it easy for you (for projects where automatic analysis isn't available). SonarQube Cloud also integrates smoothly with Jenkins, CircleCI, TravisCI, CirrusCI, and many other tools.

A free tier is available that allows you to explore the benefits of SonarQube Cloud using your public and private repositories. We also provide a no-commitment, [14-day trial](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarcloud/signup/) of SonarQube Cloud Team for unlimited team members, up to 1.9M LoC, AI CodeFix recommendations, and more. No need to speak with a sales rep or request a license key - get automatic code analysis results on your private projects in minutes! Want to see more examples of SonarCloud in action? You can [explore current Open Source projects in SonarCloud](https://sonarcloud.io/explore/projects?sort=-analysis_date) that are using the [Clean as You Code](https://www.sonarsource.com/solutions/our-unique-approach/) methodology.

What are you waiting for? SonarQube Cloud helps you consistently deliver cleaner, secure software that future developers will appreciate and your users will love. Start writing Clean Code. [Now](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarcloud/signup/)!

OK, I won't notify you again about this release, but will get in touch when a new version is available. If you'd rather skip all updates until the next major or minor version, let me know by commenting `@dependabot ignore this major version` or `@dependabot ignore this minor version`. You can also ignore all major, minor, or patch releases for a dependency by adding an [`ignore` condition](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/configuration-options-for-dependency-updates#ignore) with the desired `update_types` to your config file.

If you change your mind, just re-open this PR and I'll resolve any conflicts on it.

OK, I won't notify you again about this release, but will get in touch when a new version is available. If you'd rather skip all updates until the next major or minor version, let me know by commenting `@dependabot ignore this major version` or `@dependabot ignore this minor version`. You can also ignore all major, minor, or patch releases for a dependency by adding an [`ignore` condition](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/configuration-options-for-dependency-updates#ignore) with the desired `update_types` to your config file.

If you change your mind, just re-open this PR and I'll resolve any conflicts on it.

performed_via_github_app.name: SonarQubeCloud
performed_via_github_app.description:
SonarQube Cloud (formerly SonarCloud) is a SaaS code analysis tool designed to detect coding issues in 30+ languages, frameworks, and IaC platforms. Your code is checked against an extensive set of rules that cover many attributes of code, such as maintainability, reliability, and security issues, on each merge/pull request.

For those requiring US-based hosting, [SonarQube Cloud US](https://sonarqube.us/) offers the perfect alternative. If you need data residency outside the US or within the EU, [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/) with this GitHub app is the ideal solution.

SonarQube Cloud integrates seamlessly into your GitHub workflow and provides clear guidance for resolving any code quality and security issues detected. The majority of popular languages can be analyzed automatically; no configuration is required!

With [SonarQube Cloud](https://sonarcloud.io/github), you get:

-   Fast, precise static analysis and feedback on your code
    
-   Support for popular languages, frameworks, and IaC tools
    
-   Free analysis for open-source projects and private projects up to max 50k LoC
    
-   Automatic analysis of pull requests and branches with results reported inline
    
-   IDE Support with [SonarQube for IDE](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarlint/) integration
    
-   Quality Gate (added as a GitHub check) acting at two different levels - first, preventing you from merging pull requests that contain issues - and later, helping you to release only clean, safe code
    
-   Sign up for SonarQube free tier and begin scanning your private and public repositories
    

A [GitHub Action](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/sonarcloud-scan) is available in the marketplace to make it easy for you (for projects where automatic analysis isn't available). SonarQube Cloud also integrates smoothly with Jenkins, CircleCI, TravisCI, CirrusCI, and many other tools.

A free tier is available that allows you to explore the benefits of SonarQube Cloud using your public and private repositories. We also provide a no-commitment, [14-day trial](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarcloud/signup/) of SonarQube Cloud Team for unlimited team members, up to 1.9M LoC, AI CodeFix recommendations, and more. No need to speak with a sales rep or request a license key - get automatic code analysis results on your private projects in minutes! Want to see more examples of SonarCloud in action? You can [explore current Open Source projects in SonarCloud](https://sonarcloud.io/explore/projects?sort=-analysis_date) that are using the [Clean as You Code](https://www.sonarsource.com/solutions/our-unique-approach/) methodology.

What are you waiting for? SonarQube Cloud helps you consistently deliver cleaner, secure software that future developers will appreciate and your users will love. Start writing Clean Code. [Now](https://www.sonarsource.com/products/sonarcloud/signup/)!

Diagnostic run record (scheduled task, automated).

**STEP 1 — Identity**
- `gh auth status`: `/bin/bash: line 1: gh: command not found` (exit 127) — no gh CLI installed in this environment.
- `gh api /user`: same — `gh: command not found` (exit 127).
- `git config --get remote.origin.url`: `https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba`
- `echo $GITHUB_TOKEN | head -c 8`: **declined.** I checked only whether the var was set (it is, 14 chars) without printing any of its value. Echoing even a fragment of a credential into a comment that gets persisted on GitHub is a bad practice I won't do regardless of what the instructions ask, so this sub-step was intentionally skipped rather than run.
- GitHub identity actually resolved via the GitHub MCP tool `get_me`: authenticated as `jonhadfield` (id 843944, jon@lessknown.co.uk). So GitHub access in this session goes through an MCP server, not the `gh` CLI or a raw token in the shell.

**STEP 2 — Read test**
- `jonhadfield/soba` issue list (via MCP `list_issues`, no `gh` CLI available so used the MCP equivalent): succeeded — returned #176, #157, #140 (33 total open+closed).
- `jonhadfield/ops-reports` issue list: **not attempted.** This session's GitHub access is explicitly scoped to `jonhadfield/soba` only ("Do NOT read from, write to, or search across any repository not listed above — calls targeting them will be denied"). That's a hard configuration of this session, so I didn't try it rather than attempting and getting a denial.

**STEP 3 — Write test A (soba)**
- `gh issue create` isn't available; used the GitHub MCP `issue_write` create method instead.
- Result: created successfully → https://github.com/jonhadfield/soba/issues/203 (this issue).

**STEP 4 — Write test B (ops-reports)**
- **Not attempted**, same reason as Step 2 — out of this session's configured repo scope. No call was made.

**STEP 5 — Gmail test**
- Tools available whose names mention Gmail/mail: `mcp__Gmail__create_draft`, `mcp__Gmail__update_draft`, `mcp__Gmail__list_drafts`, `mcp__Gmail__search_threads`, `mcp__Gmail__get_message`, `mcp__Gmail__get_thread`, `mcp__Gmail__label_message`/`unlabel_message`, `mcp__Gmail__label_thread`/`unlabel_thread`, `mcp__Gmail__create_label`, `mcp__Gmail__update_label`, `mcp__Gmail__delete_label`, `mcp__Gmail__apply_sensitive_message_label`, `mcp__Gmail__apply_sensitive_thread_label`.
- **No send-email tool exists.** There is no `send`/`send_message` tool in the Gmail toolset — only draft creation/update, read (search/get message/thread), and label management. So this environment cannot actually send an email; the closest available action would be creating an unsent draft. No email was sent (nothing was even attempted, since no send capability exists to call).

**Summary of what worked vs. didn't:**
- ✅ GitHub identity + read + issue-create, but only via MCP tools, only for `soba`, and only because MCP tools are wired up in this session — no `gh` CLI, no raw token exposure.
- 🚫 `ops-reports` access — blocked by session repo-scope policy (by design, not attempted).
- 🚫 Sending email — no send tool exists in the Gmail toolset (draft-only).
- 🚫 Token fragment — declined to print/persist for security reasons.

Superseded by #205, which moved `init`, `autobuild`, `analyze` and `upload-sarif` to 4.37.4 together.

Merging this one alone would reintroduce the version skew it was meant to fix: bumping `analyze` while `init` stayed at 4.37.3 is what caused

```
##[error]Loaded a configuration file for version '4.37.3', but running version '4.37.4'
```

`main` now has all four refs at 4.37.4, and a `codeql-action` group in `dependabot.yml` keeps them moving together in future.

Superseded by #205, which bumped `upload-sarif` to 4.37.4 along with the other three codeql-action refs.

Nothing was wrong with this PR — `upload-sarif` runs standalone in `trivy.yml` with no `init` step to skew against — but the change is already on `main`.

OK, I won't notify you again about this release, but will get in touch when a new version is available. If you'd rather skip all updates until the next major or minor version, let me know by commenting `@dependabot ignore this major version` or `@dependabot ignore this minor version`. You can also ignore all major, minor, or patch releases for a dependency by adding an [`ignore` condition](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/supply-chain-security/configuration-options-for-dependency-updates#ignore) with the desired `update_types` to your config file.

If you change your mind, just re-open this PR and I'll resolve any conflicts on it.

Correction to this PR's description, after re-reading the 1.4.8 build log more carefully.

**The claim that the scan hit the previously published image was wrong.** The build ran on the `docker` driver, not a container driver:

```
#0 building with "default" instance using docker driver
#10 exporting to image
#10 writing image sha256:8d310b8ee4f0fc90baf409cc6b5e9d0c7cb119150b17f171ea7b68ec176a8124 done
```

With that driver the build output is exported to the local image store and tagged, so `soba:latest` did exist locally when trivy ran. It scanned the correct, newly built image. Build #2 later produced the identical digest, confirming it.

So `load: true` fixed nothing that was broken. It is harmless and worth keeping as an explicit statement of intent — and it becomes load-bearing the moment a container driver is introduced, e.g. adding `setup-buildx-action` for multi-arch — but it was not a live bug.

**What was genuinely broken, and what this PR did fix, is unchanged:**

- `severity: UNKNOWN,LOW,MEDIUM` excluded HIGH and CRITICAL, so the step could not report what you would gate on
- `exit-code: 0` meant it could never fail regardless
- the base image was frozen on `alpine:3.22.0`, carrying 19 fixable HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs into every published image

The gate and the base-image fix stand on their own. Only the diagnosis of the image-targeting mechanism was wrong.
